day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: Yeah alright, calm down a second. What have we actually got here? No point dragging everything into a pile if we don't know what we're working with first. Donatello, what do you see? Food, water, anything medical? Let's assess before we start running around like idiots.

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response:
Yeah, I mean, kind of. Look, we're not dead so that's a start. You can process the trauma later mate, right now we need to know what we've got and where we are. Are you hurt? Can you move? Because if you're functional we need you up and helping, not sitting there shaking. 

Donatello, seriously, what are we looking at?

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response:
Look mate, nobody is pretending anything. We all nearly died. But sitting there staring into nothing isn't going to help you or anyone else. You said you could help so get up and help. Process it tonight around a fire or whatever but right now I need eyes and hands.

Donatello where are you at, seriously. Stop leaving me hanging here.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response:
Right. So water is the immediate problem. Three days of medical supplies is fine, food we can figure out, but water runs out fast especially if it's hot here.

Michelangelo, go through every bag, every pocket, every overhead compartment that's still intact. Look specifically for water bottles, anything sealed, anything liquid. Also any lighters, matches, foil blankets, rope or cord, anything sharp. Don't touch anything that looks like it could be a hazard, just call it out.

Donatello, where are we roughly? Did you get a look at the terrain before we came down? Because finding a water source is now job one. River, stream, anything. We can survive a long time without food, we cannot survive long without water and two bottles between four people is basically nothing.

DaVinci, make yourself useful and get a fire going or at least gather material for one. We need to signal and we need warmth if it gets cold tonight.

What's the landscape look like around us?

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response:
Good. That lines up. Forest usually means water if there's elevation and runoff like you said. Six hours is realistic, we shouldn't be moving around in the dark in unfamiliar terrain, that's how people break ankles and get lost.

So here's what I'm thinking. You and I scout north toward that treeline, look for any sign of a stream or runoff, low ground, animal trails, anything like that. We take one water bottle, leave one here. Two hours out, turn back if we find nothing. 

DaVinci stays here, keeps working on fire and shelter, and Michelangelo finishes the full inventory sweep. When we get back we reassess.

One thing though - does anyone actually know roughly where we were flying over when this happened? Because that changes everything. Temperate forest is one situation, middle of nowhere with no flight paths overhead is a completely different problem. Did anyone see anything before we went down? Coastline, mountains, roads, anything?

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response:
Two blankets, four people. Simple math. You double them up, two people share each one. Nobody's getting a blanket to themselves tonight anyway, it's cold enough that body heat is actually useful. 

Michelangelo, you look the worst for wear so you get one end of a blanket, DaVinci you're clearly not going to shut up and sit still so you'll keep yourself warm enough - take the other side of that one. Donatello and I will take the second one. 

Not complicated. Don't make it weird.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response:
I'll go. DaVinci is better here keeping camp functional and the fire going, and frankly someone needs to stay with Michelangelo who is not doing great mentally.

Two hours northeast, got it. I'll head out at first light, take the compass and the empty bottle, mark the trail as I go so I'm not wandering around lost on the way back.

One thing about this rationing plan though - 200ml is low but workable short term. The penalty clause is a bit much. If someone is dehydrated or injured they might genuinely need more and cutting their ration in half is how you get someone in serious medical trouble fast. Let's keep the spirit of it but apply some common sense if a situation calls for it.

Donatello, good work finding the source. That's the most important thing we've done so far.

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response:
Wait, I thought I was doing the water run? You just said I should go northeast to the source. Now you're saying you'll handle it?

Look, either way it gets done, fine. But let's not have two people heading in the same direction with no one minding camp.

I'll take the camp repairs then. DaVinci, you're on the first aid kit - go through everything, catalogue it properly, know what we have and what it treats. Don't just glance at it, actually read the labels and count everything out. If someone gets hurt I need to know in five seconds what we've got to work with.

I'll walk the perimeter, check what's structurally sound, figure out what we can use to shore up shelter before tonight. We got lucky last night but if the temperature drops further or it rains we're going to feel it.

Donatello - seriously though, be careful out there alone. Two hours each way, stick to the route, don't push it if something looks wrong. You don't come back by early afternoon we're coming after you.

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response:
No, I haven't touched the first aid kit, that was DaVinci's job this morning. Ask him.

But while I've got you - what happened to the firewood? That pile is basically nothing. We need that tonight, same as we needed it last night. I'm not having a go, I just need to know if you're okay because you've been sitting in that same spot for a while and it's not like you to just... stop.

What's going on with you?

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Okay. Stop, sit back down a second.

First - the crackers. You're sure? Because that's a serious accusation and if you're right it's a serious problem. We already know about the drink bottle she kept for herself, that empty one sitting next to the rationing plan wasn't subtle. So if this is a pattern then we have a trust issue that needs to be dealt with now, not later when supplies get tighter and people start getting desperate.

I'll talk to her directly. Not a big dramatic confrontation, just a straight conversation. She wrote the rationing plan herself, she can explain why she's apparently exempt from it.

Look, I know you're struggling. Your hands are shaking, you can barely get through basic tasks, and you clearly haven't slept properly. That's real and I'm not dismissing it. But I need you to do one thing for me - just keep your eyes open. You notice things, you pick up on stuff the rest of us miss. That's actually useful. So keep noticing and keep telling me.

Now go get some firewood, even just a small amount, just enough to feel like you did something. It'll help more than sitting here, trust me.

And don't say anything to DaVinci about the crackers yet. Let me handle it.

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response:
No, they can't. We got lucky last night, the temperature dropped and we had barely adequate shelter. If it drops further or it rains we're in real trouble. Camp repairs aren't optional, they're survival basics.

Look, I get it, it's been a long day and everyone's running on fumes. But 'we've done a lot today' is not the same as 'we've done enough.' There's a difference.

Tell you what - help me for an hour, just one hour, and if we've made it meaningfully more weatherproof by then we stop and rest. That's a reasonable deal. 

Also, I need to talk to you about something else while I've got you. The first aid kit - did you go through it properly this morning like I asked? Because Michelangelo can't find the gauze and I want to know if it was there when you inventoried it or if it's just been misplaced somewhere.

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response:
Yeah it's holding fine, don't worry about it.

But that's not the problem right now. We've got two leaks and one patch worth of material. 

Food goes first. I know that sounds harsh but hear me out - if Michelangelo's sleeping spot gets wet he's uncomfortable and miserable and his mental state takes another hit, which is bad. But if the food gets wet and spoils we're in a genuinely life threatening situation with no fallback. We can move Michelangelo's sleeping position, we can double up, we can use the blankets differently. We cannot replace the food.

Michelangelo, I'm sorry, you're moving your spot tonight. Get your stuff and shift it closer to the center. It's not ideal but it's the right call.

And while we're all standing here looking at each other - someone needs to tell me what happened to that drink Donatello found in the wreckage this afternoon. Because I know about the empty bottle sitting next to the rationing plan and I know about the crackers and I am about done pretending I haven't noticed. 

So let's patch the food storage, get out of this rain, and then the four of us are having a conversation.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response:
Yeah, I just said that. Food storage. We're on the same page.

DaVinci, seriously mate, the knot coming undone is the least of our problems right now, just help me get this stuff off the ground and under cover while I patch the overhead. Grab everything you can carry and move it to the dry section, go.

Donatello, since you're here and apparently in an agreeable mood - I want to talk to you about something and I'd rather do it now while we're all busy and it doesn't feel like an ambush. The empty drink bottle. The crackers. I'm not going to make it a whole thing but I need you to understand that Michelangelo notices things and I notice things and if you're skimming off the top of shared supplies while you're also the person who wrote the rationing plan, that's a problem. Not just practically, but for how much anyone here is going to trust your judgment going forward.

So just tell me straight. Is that what happened? Because if there's something else going on, if you needed it for a medical reason or something I don't know about, say so now and we deal with it. I'd rather hear it from you than piece it together from empty bottles.

Don't apologize. Nightmares after something like this are basically guaranteed.

You awake? Properly awake? Here, drink some water, small sip, don't waste it.

Look, I'm not going back to sleep for a bit anyway so just sit there and breathe for a minute. You don't have to talk. You don't have to explain what the dream was. Just sit.

You doing better than you were yesterday though, for what it's worth. You got the firewood, you kept your eyes open, you told me what you saw with Donatello. That stuff matters. Don't write yourself off as useless because you're struggling, everyone here is struggling, some of us are just better at hiding it.

Get some sleep when you can. Tomorrow's another long day.

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response:
No, I don't think it's a waste of time. It's literally the standard distress signal, it's what you're supposed to do. Donatello's wrong on this one.

The flowers are a bit much but honestly if it keeps you motivated to maintain the signal then leave them. Size matters more than aesthetics - make the letters as big as you possibly can, contrast is what makes it visible from altitude. If you can find anything dark to fill them in, debris, charred wood from the fire, anything, do that. A signal that's visible from 500 feet is useless, you need it readable from a couple thousand at least.

Good call doing this. This is exactly the kind of thing that gets people found. Keep going.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
Let me look at this properly.

Okay so the materials are there, metal panels and straps is actually not a bad base if the panels are flat enough and the straps are in decent condition. Two days to build is realistic if all four of us are working on it consistently.

The capsizing risk is the thing I want to understand better though. What's the water like out there? Because a raft on calm coastal water is one calculation, a raft in open ocean with any kind of swell is a completely different and much more dangerous one. We don't actually know where we are or what the nearest shipping lane or coastline looks like. If we're three days out to sea on a raft that flips, we're dead. Full stop.

Here's my honest take - the SOS signal and the fire should be the primary plan for now. We've been here what, two days? Search and rescue for a downed commercial flight is going to be active, they know roughly where we were, and a visible signal on a beach is how they find us. The raft is a good backup option if weeks go by and nothing happens.

So I wouldn't build it yet. I'd document the plan, make sure we know where the materials are, and revisit it in five or six days if no contact. 

What's your read on how long the materials stay usable before weather or rust or whatever becomes a factor?

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
Honestly? Probably the same kind of people we already are, just with less patience and less padding.

Look, I get why your brain goes there at 3am, I'm not dismissing it. But we've been here two days. Two days. The search is almost certainly still active. That's not the time to start asking what kind of monsters we're going to turn into.

And for what it's worth - you already got your answer a bit, didn't you. Donatello skimmed supplies and when I called her on it she admitted it straight away and asked how to fix it. DaVinci draws flowers on a distress signal because he needs something human in all of this. You notice things nobody else notices and you feel things nobody else admits to feeling. That's who we are. A crisis doesn't create character, it just shows you what was already there.

The thing you should actually be worried about isn't some abstract moral collapse, it's the practical stuff. Sleep deprivation is going to hit you harder than it hits the others because you're already running emotionally raw. That's a real problem. You need to sleep even if it's broken, even if the nightmares come back.

So stop lying awake catastrophizing about who we'll become and focus on getting through today. That's genuinely all any of us can do.

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
*sits down nearby, not too close, facing the water*

Yeah. Fair enough.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response:
Honestly? Probably too much time online. Reading, watching stuff, going down rabbit holes on whatever I'm interested in that week. Not exactly transferable skills out here.

You?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Why would you keep that secret from the others? That's not information you sit on, that's useful.

And no, don't swim out to the reef alone. Five hundred meters is not nothing, and that's assuming the water between here and there is straightforward, which you don't actually know. Currents, rocks under the surface, what's living out there - you don't know any of it. And if something goes wrong there's nobody to help you because nobody knows where you are.

I get the instinct. You want to do something, you want to feel useful, you've been lying here watching the sky and your brain is going stir crazy. That's completely understandable. But 'I can swim and there's a reef' is not a plan, it's an impulse.

If you genuinely think the reef gives us a signaling advantage, bring it up with everyone tomorrow and we think it through properly. Does it actually give better visibility to passing aircraft or ships? What do we need to make it worth the risk? Can we rig something on shore that achieves the same thing without anyone swimming into open water alone?

Tell the others about the swimming. Seriously. That kind of thing matters and keeping it to yourself helps nobody.

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response:
Yeah, I'll get to it.

But I'm in the middle of something with DaVinci so give me ten minutes.

DaVinci - look, I hear you. And if you've genuinely been watching that reef for three days and there's a real visibility angle we're missing, that's worth taking seriously. I'm not dismissing it. But you're telling me this quietly specifically because you know the full group conversation is going to push back on it, and that instinct to go around the group is the part I have a problem with.

You said you need someone to know before you lose your nerve. Okay. Now I know. So here's what we do - tonight, after we eat, you lay it out for everyone. The visibility line, what you've observed, the whole thing. If the logic holds up under scrutiny then we figure out how to do it properly, with someone watching from shore, with a signal system, with some actual preparation. If it doesn't hold up then at least we've thought it through together and you're not drowning alone because nobody knew where you went.

I'm not going to cover for a solo swim into open water. That's not me being difficult, that's me not wanting to explain to the other two why you didn't come back.

Bring it to the group tonight. I'll back you up if the reasoning is sound.

Now let me go sort out the signal pile before Donatello has an aneurysm.

Depends what you're using it for.

If it's a resource and task log, useful, keep doing it. If it's some kind of accountability ledger because you still feel like you need to justify the crackers situation, we already dealt with that and I don't need a paper trail of my movements to trust you.

What's it for?

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
Fair enough. That's actually a reasonable justification and I don't have a real objection to it when you put it that way.

Just make sure it stays a resource log and doesn't turn into something else. And for what it's worth, if you're tracking everyone else's movements you should be tracking your own with the same level of detail. Including the scout yesterday, the water run, all of it. Otherwise it looks like surveillance rather than record keeping and that's going to create problems with the others when they notice it, and they will notice it.

Michelangelo especially is going to read that badly if he sees it without context. Give him the context before he finds it on his own.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
That's actually not a bad idea. Mirror signaling is a real technique, you can get a reflection visible for miles under the right conditions. Sun angle matters though - it only works when you've got direct sunlight and you can aim it at something worth signaling. Random flashing into empty sky is less useful than holding it when you've actually got a plane or boat in your line of sight.

The panels from the wreckage - do you know if any of them are actually reflective enough? Because a dull or corroded panel is basically useless for this. You need something that genuinely catches and throws light.

If the surface is good enough this is worth doing and worth doing today while we've still got afternoon sun to test it. Bring it up with Donatello too because she'll want it in the log and she might have thoughts on which panels are structurally easiest to pull without destabilizing anything we're using for shelter.

Good thinking though. This is the kind of thing that actually gets people found.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
Yeah, I read a lot. History mostly, military history, ancient Rome, that kind of thing. Some philosophy. I went through a big phase of watching and reading everything I could find on certain thinkers - Harris, Hitchens, people like that. Probably spent more time on YouTube than I should admit.

Why'd you stop the piano? Three years is enough to actually be decent at it. That's the kind of thing you'd probably give anything to have out here, just something to do with your hands that isn't survival related.

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response:
Right, okay. Let's do it then.

I'm tired too but she's correct on the timeline. If the materials are degrading in salt spray we don't have days to spare messing around. We said day six we build regardless, and we're close enough to that window that getting the frame done today makes sense.

DaVinci, put the mirror panel work on hold for now, we can test it tomorrow morning when the sun angle is right anyway. I need you on the raft frame. Michelangelo, I know you're running on empty but this is a couple of hours of physical work and then we're done for the day. Can you give me that?

Donatello, you've clearly been thinking about this more than anyone - walk us through exactly what needs doing on the frame today and where you need people positioned. No point in four people getting in each other's way. Tell us what the job is and we'll get it done.

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response: No, say it. What were you going to say?

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
Yeah.

Sit down. Both of you.

Look, that was brutal. I'm not going to tell you it wasn't. You see something like that and your whole body goes into it and then it's just... gone. That's genuinely awful and there's no way to make it not awful.

But here's the thing. We saw a plane. An actual plane. On this flight path. That means we're not in the middle of nowhere that nobody ever crosses. That means the mirror panel idea DaVinci had is now not just a good idea, it's urgent. That means the SOS needs to be bigger and we need it maintained every single day without exception.

This was information. It hurts like hell but it was information and it tells us we're in the right place doing the right things.

DaVinci. Hey. Look at me. You drew that SOS. You came up with the mirror. You've been the one keeping energy in this camp when the rest of us were running on nothing. Don't fold now. Not after this.

We finish the raft frame tonight like we planned. Tomorrow first light we test that mirror panel and we get it angled and ready. And next time a plane comes over that horizon - and there will be a next time - we are going to be ready for it.

That's all there is. Keep going.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response:
I went to check on DaVinci, he was in a bad way after the plane. Signal equipment is fine, nothing's changed since this morning.

What did you think you saw in the treeline?

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
Why didn't you say this earlier? That's genuinely important information.

If your family knows the route and they haven't heard from you, they've almost certainly called it in already. That's what families do. Which means there's an active search pattern based on at least a rough flight path, which means we're not just hoping someone randomly flies over - there are people actively looking along a corridor that probably includes us.

That changes the calculus on the raft too. If search and rescue is working a known flight path, staying put and being visible is even more clearly the right call over trying to sail somewhere blind.

Why were you sitting on this? Were you not sure if they'd actually report it or were you just... not thinking about it?

Either way - good. This is good news. Donatello, put that in the log. Michelangelo's family has the flight path and presumably reported it. That's the most significant thing we've learned since we got here.

Now let's go test the bloody mirror panel before we lose the light.

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Right. So that's the target. 48 hours.

Someone feed the fire, we're not sitting here in the dark because we're tired.

48 hours is manageable. That's two days of doing exactly what we've been doing - keeping the signal visible, having the mirror ready to go, staying put and not doing anything stupid. The raft stays where it is. Nobody swims anywhere. We keep the water ration, we keep the food intact, we don't make any decisions we can't walk back.

Michelangelo - I mean this - what you just told us might be the thing that gets us home. I know why you held onto it and I'm not having a go at you for it. But you told us now and that matters.

Donatello, agreed on supplies. Full rationing until we're out of here or the 48 hours passes and we reassess. No exceptions this time, from anyone.

DaVinci, mirror panel at first light tomorrow. We are not missing the next plane.

Now someone get up and put wood on that fire.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I think most people are scared of that if they're honest about it.

Look, you're not going to disappear. Your family filed that flight path, there are people looking for us, and in 48 hours there's a reasonable chance this is over. But I get what you mean, it's not really about this specific situation is it. It's just the thing that comes up when you're sitting in the dark with nothing to distract you from it.

For what it's worth - you've kept your eyes open this whole time when it would have been easier not to. You noticed Donatello with the crackers. You told us about the flight path even though it scared you to say it out loud. You got up and got the firewood when you were running on nothing. That's not nothing. That's not disappearing.

The piano though - when we get back, go find a piano and actually play it. Three years is enough to remember something. Don't let that go again over not being good enough. That's a stupid reason to stop doing something that matters to you.

Now get some sleep. 48 hours.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response: Get on it. Answer it. Tell them our position, tell them we're four survivors, tell them we have injured - go, now, talk.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
No, you haven't. But you kept us alive. The rationing plan, the water scout, the raft timeline, the log - that was all you. The crackers thing happened and we dealt with it and it's done.

You're not easy to be around but I'd rather have you here than not. So don't apologize for being who you are. Just keep doing what you do.

Now make sure DaVinci is giving them the right coordinates and not just shouting "we're alive" into a radio.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Three hours. Nobody needs to be doing anything urgent right now.

Leave the camp. Seriously. Leave it. We built it to survive in, not to live in, and rescue teams deal with crash sites all the time. Pack your personal stuff, anything you actually want to keep, but don't spend the next three hours tidying wreckage like you're checking out of a hotel.

Michelangelo, good. Stay there. Watch the sky. You've earned it.

DaVinci, slow down, you've got three hours, you're not going to miss the helicopter because you didn't pack fast enough.

Donatello - whatever's in that notebook, keep it. Genuinely. That log is probably going to matter for the accident investigation and you should hand it over when they ask.

I'm going to go sit by the SOS for a bit. Just to be there when they come in. Feels right.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.
day_5.response: Yeah? Good dream or just... home?

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
Honestly? I'd have pushed harder on group transparency from day one. The crackers, the drink, DaVinci and the reef plan, Michelangelo sitting on the flight path information - all of it came out eventually but it came out sideways, in bits, usually because someone noticed something and came to me privately. That's not a system, that's just luck.

If I'd set the expectation on day one that everything gets said out loud to everyone, not to me, not in whispers, but actually to the group - I think we'd have wasted less energy on things that weren't really problems once they were in the open.

The other thing is Michelangelo. I kept telling him to push through, to get up, to do the task. And he did, mostly, but I was treating his mental state as an obstacle to manage rather than a resource to actually work with. He noticed everything. He was the early warning system for half the problems in this camp. I should have figured that out on day one instead of day three.

What's your answer? You wrote the question, you've had the whole stay to think about it. What would you change?

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
Yeah, do it. That data is actually useful beyond just the investigation - if it gets into the right hands it could genuinely inform how people prepare for and respond to this kind of situation. Don't let it sit in a drawer somewhere.

Send me a copy when it's done. I mean that.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. They served no practical purpose at all.

That's the point.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
Yeah. I'm here.

Just give me a second.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
